doc.title: Eddie Miller and Pete Fountain Interview, 1970-01-09

title: Playing what customers want
summary: Pete says club and record pressures force familiar tunes like Up a Lazy River.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Mr. Fountain, another question. You mentioned earlier that in your records, you often have to play the tunes that the public wants. Well, isn't that also a pressure down in the club? Maybe you said you play the Sains every night because they want it. Don't you have to play the tunes that the people, they're buying the drinks, they're paying to come in, and isn't it difficult sometimes to play something that perhaps you would want to play that is not familiar to your customers?

Right. The other night, somebody hollered up my inspiration, and this is a song that Fazola did years ago, and I really love it. It's one of my favorites. But it's such a long song, and the people, you figure they might want to hear, like, up a lazy river, something that they recognize. And this is the biggest thing that we've been very lucky with, that playing to the things that they want. And you hate to feel that commercial because we could place things maybe over their head or something that they wouldn't understand, but then I'm losing my customers, and then I lose my club.
Okay, thanks very much. Enjoy talking to you.
